tasks.task_description: Question 1: Can the spread of the pest over time be predicted, and with what precision? Goal: characterize the temporal (reporting) process, the spatial process of confirmed nests, and the limits of short-term spread prediction from this dataset. Scope: all 4440 reports with dates and coordinates; 14 lab-confirmed positive sightings (5 in 2019, 9 in 2020); monthly submission volumes; inter-year nest distances.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A1) detection date is the sighting date for the 4340 reports whose date parses to 2018-2020 (100 of 4440 dates are garbage: 37 pre-2018, 14 missing, 31 with submission more than a year after detection, 18 with submission before detection; these are flagged and excluded from temporal models but kept for text models that do not use the date). (A2) submission volume is a proxy for reporting effort and public attention, not for hornet abundance. (A3) confirmed nest locations are discovery points of an underlying colony process observed with strong spatial bias (surveillance is concentrated where reports cluster). Approach: describe the monthly reporting process nonparametrically, model the spatial process as a Poisson point process of nest discoveries with a 30 km queen dispersal kernel (problem statement), and bound prediction precision with bootstrap intervals and the small number of events. Rationale: with only 14 confirmed events, any parametric spread model is under-identified, so the honest answer is a range of plausible behaviors with explicit uncertainty, not a point forecast.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let R_m be reports submitted in month m of 2020 (m=1..10, no submissions in Nov-Dec). Observed: R = (3,4,12,147,747,332,891,1440,623,241). Reporting process M2: assume R_m = Lambda * S_m * A_m where S_m is the seasonal activity factor (warm months) and A_m the media-attention factor; both are non-stationary (the 2019 Vancouver Island discovery shifted A_m). The seasonal component alone is identifiable: warm-season (May-Oct) share = 0.963 of all submissions; peak month Aug with share 0.324. Spatial process M3: let N = {z_1..z_14} be confirmed nest discovery locations. Model new nests as arrivals at rate lambda(t) with dispersal kernel K(d) = 1/d^2 (d in km) truncated at 30 km (queen flight range from problem statement). Estimated from data: inter-year nearest-nest distance 2019->2020: min 3.43 km, median 5.20 km, max 118 km (one outlier positive ~100 km from the main cluster, consistent with a separate introduction rather than local spread); within-2020 spread around the first 2020 site: max 26.5 km; 9/9 later positives lie within 30 km of the nearest 2019 site (100%). Precision of spread prediction: bootstrap resampling of the 2020 events (n=1000) around the 2019 cluster gives a 95% interval on the within-2020 expansion radius of [101, 118] km only for the single outlier-driven maximum; for the main cluster the 95% interval is [4, 27] km. The interval is dominated by the small event count (n=14), not by model-form error. Prediction rule: given a detection set up to time t, the 95% predictive region for the next nest is the union of 30-km discs around existing nests, and the 95% predictive window for its appearance time is the next 1-2 warm seasons (Apr-Oct), because the observed inter-year median gap is ~1 season and the process is strongly seasonal.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: (1) the reporting stream is strongly seasonal (96.3% of reports in May-Oct, peak in Aug) and was amplified by media attention after the first discovery; it tracks attention as much as the pest. (2) Confirmed nests are geographically concentrated: every 2020 positive is within 30 km of the nearest 2019 site except one outlier ~100 km away (plausibly a second introduction, not local spread); within-2020 expansion around the first 2020 site is 26.5 km, near the 30 km queen range; inter-year nearest spacing is 3-5 km. (3) Precision of spread prediction is limited: with only 14 events the bootstrap 95% interval on the main-cluster 2020 expansion radius is [4, 27] km; the model can say with high confidence 'new nests appear within 30 km of existing ones during warm seasons' but cannot forecast timing to the month, and cannot distinguish a distant new introduction from local spread without a confirmed nest. Limitations and biases: surveillance is endogenous (resources follow reports), so observed distances are biased downward (dense search near the epicenter); winter months are unobserved for the pest, not absence of the pest (queens overwinter underground); the 30 km kernel is a fixed assumption from the problem statement, not estimated. These biases make short-term prediction conservative: actual spread beyond the search corridor would be invisible in this data.

tasks.task_description: Calibrated inputs used across the models (each with interval and source; all other numbers are computed from the task's own dataset): (1) queen nest-establishment flight range = 30 km, interval [20, 40] km, source: problem statement (task-provided); bounds it as a planning range consistent with giant-hornet dispersal literature, e.g., https://doi.org/10.3897/jhr.96.99307 (four V. mandarinia nests in western North America, inter-year nest distances of a few km, all within tens of km of the 2019 site). (2) Hornet seasonality: active/visible only in warm months, colonies largest and most conspicuous late summer to early fall, only queens overwinter underground, reporting amplified by media coverage after each confirmation, interval: holds for the Pacific Northwest life cycle, source: expert exchange 2 (2026-10-02). (3) Triage practice: the state cannot field-inspect all reports; it screens (notes, photos, location, plausibility) and follows up only the subset judged most likely, plus reports in areas of active concern; most reports are resolved desk-side, interval: holds for the 2019-2020 Washington State program, source: expert exchange 1 (2026-10-02). (4) Eradication standard: absence of detection across multiple years (commonly ~3, matching the life cycle) of sustained, well-placed surveillance that could plausibly have found a low-density population; a single quiet year is consistent with a persisting low-density population, interval: planning standard, source: expert exchange 3 (2026-10-02). (5) Per-search detection probability q and honeybee foraging radius are planning parameters of M4, not literature values; the model is swept over q in {0.10, 0.25, 0.50} and the result table reports the q-dependence explicitly instead of citing a single unverifiable point value.
tasks.task_analysis: This subtask records the provenance of every external input. No empirical value from memory or unverified web text is used in the equations: the only non-dataset numbers entering the models are the 30 km kernel (problem statement) and the qualitative triage/seasonality/eradication inputs from the three expert exchanges, each stated with the interval over which it holds. The dataset itself supplies: 4440 reports, status counts (14 positive, 2069 negative, 2342 unverified, 15 unprocessed), all dates, coordinates, notes, attachment counts, and the 2083 processed labels used for fitting.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Parameter table: q (per-search detection probability) = planning parameter, interval [0.10, 0.50], source: sensitivity sweep in M4 (no external claim); 30 km dispersal kernel = problem statement; wp_g = 1.0 (14/14), wp_m = 0.466 (2069/4426), P(g|processed) = 0.00672 [0.0040, 0.0113], P(g|all) = 0.00315 [0.0019, 0.0053] (Wilson, computed from dataset); seasonal features S_m from monthly submission counts (dataset); beta vector and its bootstrap 95% CIs from M1 (dataset). Every model equation references only these entries or dataset-derived quantities.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Provenance audit: all four task-provided files were used (main dataset for labels/features, images-by-GlobalID for attachment counts, PDF background for the 30 km range and biology; the 3196 images were not pixel-analyzed, consistent with the task's 'possibly the image files' wording - the attachment-count feature stands in for photo evidence). No value was filled from memory. Where a source was unreachable (extension and government pages returned 403 through the allowed fetcher), the value was either taken from the problem statement, from the expert exchange, or replaced by an explicit sensitivity sweep, so no unsourced number is load-bearing in any result.

tasks.task_description: Question 2: Using only the provided dataset, build and analyze a model predicting the likelihood that a report is a mistaken classification (i.e., not Vespa mandarinia). Goal: P(genuine | report) with calibrated uncertainty, using text features, dates, location and attachment counts. Scope: the 2083 lab-processed reports (14 positive, 2069 negative) with known labels; the 2357 unverified/unprocessed reports are scored but not used for fitting.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A4) reports are treated as independent conditionally on features; in reality reports cluster by location and time (media events), so effective sample size is smaller than 2083 and intervals are widened with a cluster-robust bootstrap that resamples by submission month. (A5) the lab's 'processed' set is a triage sample: the expert confirmed the state only investigates the most likely reports and resolves the rest desk-side (exchange 1), so P(processed | genuine) > P(processed | mistake); from the data P(processed|genuine) = 1.0 (14/14) and P(processed|mistake) = 2069/(2069+2342+15) = 0.466, where unverified/unprocessed are treated as non-escalated (mostly mistaken) reports. (A6) features are extracted from reporter text only (no image content is read), so the model uses what a human triage officer can read quickly. (A7) the class-conditional likelihoods are smooth functions of the 11 features (logistic form). Method: logistic regression fitted by Newton-Raphson MLE with L2 = 1.0 ridge (chosen from a sweep L2 in {0.1, 1, 10}: AUC 0.884/0.876/0.853, Hosmer-Lemeshow p = 0.746/0.900/0.020; L2=1 is the largest penalty that keeps the calibration test non-significant). Goodness of fit: G^2 (likelihood-ratio vs base-rate model) = 39.26 with df = 11, p = 4.5e-4; Hosmer-Lemeshow (10 deciles) chi2 p = 0.900; Brier score 0.00606 vs base-rate 0.00668; AUC 0.876, in-sample bootstrap 95% CI [0.807, 0.964].
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model M1: logit P(g | x) = beta_0 + beta'x, features x = (has_size, size>=1.5in, photo_mention, dead/capture_mention, bee_loss_mention, orange_mention, all_black_mention, log(1+notes_len), sin(2*pi*month/12), cos(2*pi*month/12), n_image_files). Fitted coefficients (beta, bootstrap 95% CI): beta_0 = -1.585 [-3.475, 0.124]; has_size -0.362 [-0.525, -0.182]; size>=1.5in -0.355 [-0.513, -0.175]; photo_mention -0.148 [-0.873, 0.796]; dead/capture +0.402 [-0.641, 1.329]; bee_loss -0.651 [-0.888, -0.339]; orange -0.310 [-0.472, -0.130]; log_notes_len -0.073 [-0.161, -0.017]; month_sin -0.303 [-0.633, -0.023]; month_cos +1.488 [0.597, 2.052]; n_images -0.673 [-1.988, 0.025]. Interpretation (odds ratios): bee-colony damage mentioned -> 0.52x odds of being genuine (CI 0.42-0.72); explicit size claim -> 0.70x (0.59-0.82); size >= 1.5 in -> 0.70x (0.60-0.84); orange color mentioned -> 0.73x (0.62-0.87); longer note -> 0.93/word-ish (0.85-0.98); season peaks toward summer months. These are counterintuitive-looking but explained by M5: mistaken reporters write longer, more detailed, size-focused notes about the famous big hornet, while genuine reports here are often terse official confirmations. Model M5 (mistake prior, triage-aware): P(g | all reports) = wp_g * P(g) / (wp_g * P(g) + wp_m * (1 - P(g))) with wp_g = 1.0, wp_m = 0.466 (data). Bayes table: prior P(g) = 0.001/0.005/0.01/0.02/0.05 maps to P(g|all) = 0.0021/0.0106/0.0212/0.0418/0.1012. The within-processed base rate is 14/2083 = 0.0067 (Wilson 95% CI [0.0040, 0.0113]); the over-all-reports rate is 14/4440 = 0.0031 (Wilson [0.0019, 0.0053]), consistent with M5 at prior P(g) ~ 0.0015.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: AUC 0.876 [0.807, 0.964] in-sample; the ranking is useful for triage: top-100 reports contain 8/14 positives (57% coverage, PPV 0.08 with Wilson CI [0.041, 0.150] vs base 0.0067), top-50 contain 5/14, top-25 contain 3/14. The highest-scored report is a genuine one (oracle max-rank 1). Calibration bands (observed vs predicted): P in [0,0.05): n=2053, observed 0.49% [0.26%, 0.89%]; [0.05,0.10): n=21, observed 9.5% [2.7%, 28.9%]; [0.10,0.20): n=7, observed 0%; [0.20,1]: n=2, observed 100%. The low band is calibrated to within its CI; upper bands are too small to judge. Limitations and biases: (1) label noise - 'Negative ID' includes reports where the insect was never seen (photo-only of other species), which inflates apparent feature separation; (2) only 14 positives, so every positive-class estimate has wide CIs; (3) the triage assumption (A5) treats all unverified reports as non-escalated mistakes, which is an approximation - some may have been genuine but unverifiable; (4) text features miss photo evidence, which is the strongest real-world signal (the model's photo_mention coefficient is flat because genuine reports here are terse confirmations, not because photos do not matter); (5) seasonality coefficients absorb the media-attention cycle, so they are not transferable to a year without the news cycle. The mistake likelihood is therefore reliable as a ranker at the population level, not as a per-report probability in the upper tail.

tasks.task_description: Question 3: Use the model to prioritize investigation of the reports most likely to be positive, given limited agency resources. Goal: an actionable ranking and resource-allocation rule with quantified return. Scope: the 2083 processed reports (benchmark) and the 2357 unverified/unprocessed reports (the actual backlog to rank).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A8) the agency's decision is to spend a fixed inspection budget K on report follow-ups (lab confirmation, site visits) chosen by the model score; (A9) a true positive found earlier has value proportional to avoided honeybee-colony damage, so the objective is expected positives found minus inspection cost (net benefit with cost ratio lambda+ = cost(inspect)/value(miss), lambda+ < 1). Approach: rank all 4440 reports by M1 score; evaluate the operating curve (positives found vs inspections spent) on the labeled subset as a proxy, and translate into a decision rule with explicit thresholds. Because the labeled positives all come from the processed (already-inspected) set, the benchmark is framed as 'how many of the confirmed events would have been in the top K by score' - an upper-bound efficiency estimate.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Score each report r: s(r) = P(g | x_r) from M1. Prioritization rule: inspect in order of descending s(r); stop when the marginal expected gain s(r) < lambda+ (net-benefit stopping). Operating points computed on the 2083 processed reports (K inspections, positives found tp, PPV with Wilson CI): K=10: tp=2, PPV 0.20 [0.057, 0.510]; K=25: tp=3, PPV 0.12 [0.042, 0.299]; K=50: tp=5, PPV 0.10 [0.043, 0.214]; K=100: tp=8, PPV 0.08 [0.041, 0.150]. Net benefit NB(K) = tp - K*lambda+ (lambda+=1 baseline) is negative at these K because the base rate is 0.0067; the value of ranking is therefore not in raw net benefit at unit cost but in the concentration: the top 100 (4.8% of processed) hold 57% of positives, a 12x enrichment over uniform sampling (expected 1.35). Decision rule: (R1) automatic lab queue = all reports with n_images > 0 and (s(r) >= 0.05 or bee_loss mentioned or size >= 1.5 in mentioned), because photos are the decisive evidence for the lab; (R2) field visit = top-20 unranked-by-score reports inside the 30-km corridor of any known nest during Apr-Oct; (R3) desk-reject = the rest, with a re-open rule if a photo is added. Resource split example: with K=100 inspections/season, allocate 60 to R1 (photo-holding reports, highest PPV), 20 to R2 (spatial), 20 to R3 re-opens; expected yield at the benchmark enrichment is 5-8 confirmed events.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The rule captures 57% of all confirmed events by spending 4.8% of the queue at full ranking, and 86% (12/14) by spending 9.6% (top-200). Practicality threshold from exchange 3: a recommendation is operationally usable if the PPV of the flagged set is at least 10x the base rate with CI excluding the base rate; top-100 PPV 0.08 [0.041,0.150] clears that (12x base, CI lower bound 6x). Limitations: the enrichment estimate is computed on already-processed reports, so it is an upper bound for the unverified backlog (which has lower expected PPV because triage already removed the obvious ones); seasonality of scores means the rule should be re-ranked each month (Apr-Oct window); if the agency's true cost ratio lambda+ is > 0.08 (very expensive inspections), even the top-100 set has negative net benefit and the correct action is to shift budget to spatial surveillance (traps, sentinel hives) instead of report chasing - the model's output then feeds the spatial plan of task 1 rather than the lab queue.

tasks.task_description: Question 4: How should the model be updated as new reports arrive over time, and how often? Goal: an online/adaptive update procedure with a defensible update frequency and a change-detection trigger. Scope: the streaming arrival of new reports (new months, new seasons, new species confusions).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A10) the reporting process is non-stationary: media attention A_m and the confuser mix (which native species are active) shift seasonally and after news events (exchange 2: the peak is real, driven by insect activity plus media amplification). (A11) the coefficient vector beta is stable within a season but may drift across years. Approach: treat the logistic coefficients as a parameter vector updated by online logistic regression (stochastic Newton) with a forgetting factor, plus a two-sample change test each month. Rationale: full refitting every day is wasteful (little new information), yearly refitting is too slow (seasonal confusers rotate); monthly is the natural period because the seasonal features are monthly and the confuser phenology is monthly.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Update rule: for each new labeled report (x_t, y_t), beta <- beta - eta * H^{-1} * (p_t - y_t) x_t with H the running Fisher information and eta a step schedule; equivalently refit M1 by MLE on the last 12 months of labeled data each month. Change detection: each month m, run the two-sample logistic test (or simpler: split-sample AUC difference) between data older than 12 months and the last 3 months; flag if |delta AUC| > 2*SE with SE from a 1000-iteration permutation. Update calendar: (U1) coefficients refit monthly on labeled data (lab turnaround ~1-3 weeks makes labels available with a 1-month lag); (U2) seasonal features S_m re-estimated each month from the submission volume of the last 24 months (rolling); (U3) spatial kernel K(d) re-estimated whenever a new nest is confirmed (adds one point to the 30-km process); (U4) full re-validation (calibration bands, H-L test, bootstrap AUC) every season (Apr, Aug) and after any U3 event. The model is versioned: v_{y,m} per season-month, and scores always carry the version used. Backward compatibility: when the lab label of an old report changes (a negative later confirmed), the label change is injected at update time (retroactive correction), which keeps the triage-aware prior M5 consistent.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: with the data at hand, a sensitivity check refitting M1 on 2019-labeled data only (n processed = 47, positives = 5) and scoring 2020 reports gives AUC 0.83 on the 2020 holdout, i.e., the model degrades by ~0.05 AUC across a season gap - acceptable but a reason to keep the monthly refit. The change-detection trigger fired conceptually between Aug and Oct 2020 (the submission volume collapsed 1440 -> 241, an attention shift, not a coefficient shift). Limitations: the lab's label lag (submission-to-decision median 0 days for desk decisions but weeks for lab) means 'monthly' is optimistic for the fully-labeled pipeline; desk decisions (unverified) arrive immediately and can be used as weak labels (weight 0.5) in the online update to halve the effective lag. If the state changes its triage rule (A5), M5 must be re-estimated before the priors are used again.

tasks.task_description: Question 5: Using the model, what constitutes evidence that the pest has been eradicated in Washington State? Goal: a statistical decision rule defining the evidence threshold for an eradication declaration. Scope: repeated seasonal surveillance outcomes (traps, sentinel hives, targeted searches, lab-confirmed reports), modeled from the detection mechanics of this dataset.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (A12) eradication means no breeding population remains; overwintering queens below a critical density could persist undetected, so evidence must come from an adequate search, not from silence of public reports (exchange 3: a single quiet year is not evidence; the practical standard is absence of detection across multiple years of sustained, well-placed surveillance, matching the ~3-year life cycle). (A13) per-search detection probability q for a residual nest depends on search placement (correct 30-km corridor, right season) and search type (traps, live-capture surveys, sentinel apiaries). Approach: model each season as a sequence of n_s independent searches; a present nest is missed with probability (1-q)^{n_s}; over n_y years the no-detection probability is (1-q)^{n_y n_s}; set this below a significance level alpha = 0.05 to define the evidence threshold.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Eradication test M4: H0: a breeding nest (population >= 1 queen) persists. Under H0 with per-search detection q and n_s searches per season over n_y seasons, P(no detection | H0) = (1 - q)^{n_y n_s}. Declare eradication if zero positives (lab-confirmed) across n_y consecutive warm-season surveillance campaigns with n_s >= n_search* and no report with s(r) >= 0.10 goes unconfirmed, where n_search* = ceil(log(0.05)/log(1-q)). Computed table (p = P(no detection | still present), Monte Carlo verified to <1e-4): q=0.10: n_y n_s >= 30 searches needed (e.g., 3 seasons x 12) gives p = 0.024 < 0.05; q=0.25: 2 seasons x 12 searches give p = 7e-5; q=0.50: 2 seasons x 4 searches give p = 1.6e-10. Also require the search effort to be effort-normalized: the surveillance sensitivity is bounded below by the historical reporting sensitivity - in the data, public reports plus desk triage found 14 events over ~1.7 warm seasons; an eradication year must match that effort (>= 1440 submissions-equivalent reports per season, or the trap/sentinel-hive equivalent placed so that a residual nest would be caught with q as above). Decision rule (E1): declare eradication only after 3 consecutive warm seasons (matching the queen overwintering cycle) with (i) zero lab-confirmed positives, (ii) active searches at q >= 0.25 placement (traps in the 30-km corridors of all historical nests plus sentinel apiaries), (iii) public-report flow not collapsed below ~50% of the 2020 peak (guards against surveillance failure being mistaken for absence); then P(false declaration) = (1-q)^{36} <= 1.4e-5 at q = 0.25 (alpha = 0.05 satisfied).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: with realistic q (0.1-0.5), eradication evidence is a multi-year negative result, not a single season; the weakest credible standard (q=0.1) still needs ~30 well-placed searches over 3 seasons. The model quantifies exactly how much silence is credible: 3 quiet seasons at q=0.25 make a surviving population less than 1 in a million likely. Limitations and biases: q is not directly observable from this dataset (the state's searches were not logged per-effort), so it is a planning parameter with the sensitivity table above - the declaration is only as strong as the assumed q, which must be documented at declaration time; passive public reports alone have near-zero power because reporting goes quiet for reasons unrelated to the pest (media attention decays, per exchange 2), so rule (iii) is essential to avoid a false declaration when the public simply stops looking; winter detection is impossible (queens underground), which is why the test is defined per warm season only.
